title: The Rise of Travel Sports and the Decline of Civic Institutions
author: Aaron Renn
summary: Aaron Renn's weekly digest opens with an extended discussion of a New York magazine feature on the "pay-to-play childhood," using it to argue that travel sports have become another K-shaped institution—one product for affluent families, a degraded alternative for everyone else—accelerated by private equity's roll-up of the youth-sports industry (Varsity Brands changing hands from $1.5 billion to $4.5 billion in a decade). He connects this to a broader thesis about civic infrastructure being liquidated for cash: rec leagues run by nonprofits and church ministries, he argues, represent exactly the kind of intermediary institution that gets hollowed out when everything becomes a for-profit product, though he points to counterexamples like the Carmel Dads' Club and Tabernacle Presbyterian's century-old recreation ministry as evidence the trend isn't total. The digest then pivots through several loosely related items: declining public standards (phone speakers on London transit), the scarcity of honest direct feedback for executives and young people alike, a data tool for finding favorable marriage markets, and a partisan breakdown of Senate staffers by gender. Renn ties these together as symptoms of the same institutional erosion—civic, familial, and mentorship structures all thinning out. It is archived here as the digest's own editorial entry (Renn as author/curator), covering family formation, childhood institutions, and civic decline central to the Family category.
points: Uses a New York magazine feature on "pay-to-play" travel sports to argue youth sports have bifurcated into a K-shaped system that erodes cross-class civic interaction.

Traces the private-equity roll-up of youth sports, including Varsity Brands' resale from $1.5 billion to $4.5 billion over a decade, as a case study in extracting cash from formerly civic-run institutions.
Points to counterexamples—the Carmel Dads' Club and church recreation ministries—as evidence that low-cost civic rec leagues persist even as high-dollar travel teams grow.
Links a Financial Times piece on paid executive mentorship to a broader argument that honest, direct feedback is increasingly scarce for both executives and young people.
Closes with marriage-market data (an Institute for Family Studies interactive map) and a partisan gender breakdown of Senate staffers, tying declining institutions to declining family formation.
quotes: It's another example of the K-shaped society in which there's one product for the affluent and a different one for everybody else.
Investors saw an opportunity and had a model. In 2014, a pair of private-equity firms acquired Varsity Brands, a team-sports-apparel and competitive-cheer company, for $1.5 billion.
I don't think it's any secret that part of the financial strategy of these groups is to build a monopolistic or oligopolistic position where they have leverage to extract more cash.
But we do have to recognize that this is just another example of civic infrastructure being treated as a standing reserve to be liquidated for cash money.
As I've written about many times before, one of the world's most valuable commodities is honest, direct, negative feedback.
I do believe there's a shortage of young men and women as individuals who are getting a tough kick in the pants from a trusted parent, pastor, boss, or teacher with skin in their game.
Another institution that's been in decline is marriage, with family formation rates falling.
